Erik Haugsjaa wrote:
> 
(snip)

> Should have all the literal instances.  So, you think there is a
> ghost writer for ISAIF?   Wouldn't this have come up in a trial?
> I'm guessing it would have been obvious from looking at all his
> other writing.

	One would think it would.  However, no passages on the development his
ideas or the acts of writing the FC documents have been released.  If
anyone contributed (perhaps only in a discussion by mail) the fact could
have been obscured by destruction or re-writing of journals, or it may
be that neither side had anything to gain.  TK would not want his
lawyers to reveal such a thing.  Prosecutors might have felt it
counterproductive, since they could not charge anyone with a crime
("felonious political conversation"?) and did not want to detract from
TK's responsibility.

> 
> If not, how does his "worldview changing" change the diagnosis of
> TK in a meaningful way?  This (his reading more books and
> explaining away his anger with "frustration agression theory")
> doesn't wipe away the very good points Johnson makes, does it?
> His delusional, antisocial and paranoid thinking still stands.
> IOW, his overall philosophy hasn't changed.... just his own
> understanding and refinement of it.  This doesn't change his
> psychiatric diagnosis or affect his desire to bomb.

	I am primarily concerned with the "rigidity" attribute, and the
persistently negative attitude.  These fit with the pattern of invoking
ideas about system, frustration, and technique.  Incorporating new ideas
without reducing them to the old categories, recognizing the value of
the positive, and making theoretical compromises (the theories of
Johnson and Skocpol, for instance, polar opposites, and very different
from frustration-aggression theorists) does not fit with the image that
emerges from the report.  So, I am interested in how a psychologist or
psychiatrist would account for this.  I cannot say that is impossible,
only that I would like to understand more.
> 
> It seems inevitable that ISAIF was going to be written.  Too many
> ideas boiling- over in his head and in his journal not to share --
> if not to save the world, then at least to please himself with his
> cleverness at making sense of this crazy world.

	Do we know anything about his ideas apart from ISAIF?  The released
portions of his cabin writings suggest nothing about his intellectual
life.

> 
> OK, so it's likely that a person can't live in the woods for that
> great a length without feeling attached to it.  I still contend
> that this is secondary to his desire to rip down industrial
> society because it means more people, noise, and restrictions on
> his freedom.  I mean... look how he can't getting in a jab at
> "social control"!

	Exactly.  The negative orientation we see in the cabin excerpts fits
with this thrust of ISAIF, with what we hear from those who knew him,
with the 1971 essay, and with the psychiatric report.  Interestingly,
the "positive" goal is identified as being something held by other
people "already," not as something the author actually believes.  The
judgments that it is best to "dump the whole stinking system" and that
"The factories should be destroyed, technical books burned, etc." is
clearly the opinion of the author.
> 
> Any advice for good reads on "frustration agression theory" or any
> of these other things you guys (Richard, the anarchist?) are
> talking about?

	The original is John Dollard "Frustration and Aggression."  It is quite
readable, and you will not doubt that the author of ISAIF read it. 
There is lots of talk about "surrogate" and "primitive" and the use of
this theory to explain shortcomings in US society, as well as the
propensity to murder.

	However, a shorter version, more relevant to revolution, is found in
the Graham and Gurr book cited in ISAIF "History of Violence in
America."
